p: Thank you, Chair Krishnan. I'm now going to ask, um, Council Member Morano to make a brief statement on his legislation.

Thank you, Chair Schulman. I appreciate your leadership, uh, Chairing this hearing and for your passion for health issues in general, uh, not just, uh, Chairing this Committee but literally your entire career in government. C I want to thank the Committee and Chair and the Speaker for, uh, your willingness to hear Intro 831 today. This is, uh, this bill is a new version of a bill that, uh, some folks in the Administration and in the, uh, labor movement had raised a couple of objections with, with respect to collective bargaining. I think this version of the bill is largely clear of any of those pitfalls. In general, the bill is about something very simple but very important. Removing a barrier for

people who are willing to save someone else's life. Right now, there are thousands of people, including many New Yorkers, waiting for organ transplants. Many of them are on dialysis, sometimes for years, hoping for a second chance, hoping for more time with their families. At the same time, there are people willing to step up to donate a kidney, part of their liver, or bone marrow, but they hesitate for one very practical reason: they can't afford to take time off from work. That's the problem we're trying to solve. Intro 831 ensures that workers across New York City have job-protected time off if they choose to become a living organ or bone marrow donor, up to 20 days for organ donation and 5 days for bone marrow, which is what the health guidelines, uh, recommend. And just as importantly, it establishes a pathway for the the city to provide wage replacement so that people are not financially penalized for doing something extraordinary. Because in plain English, this is what it comes down to: if you're willing to go through surgery to save someone's life, you shouldn't have to worry about losing your paycheck. This bill recognizes something fundamental: that the biggest

barrier to organ donation is often not willingness, it's reality. It's time off work, it's recovery, it's making rent, it's supporting your family. This legislation is about removing that barrier so more people can step up. And I'll tell you, uh, the issue is very personal for me because for years, first on the radio and now as a Council Member, I've heard from people waiting for transplants, people stuck on dialysis, people hoping for, for that call that could change everything. And I've also seen what happens when that call comes. A close friend of mine received, ah, a liver transplant about a decade ago. Transplant gave him 10 more years of life, 10 more years with his family, 10 more years with his friends, 10— that time that meant just everything and that's what organ donation does. It gives people time. It gives families memories that they otherwise wouldn't have. This bill, uh, has evolved through the legislative process, and I appreciate the input from the Administration and from my colleagues and from the labor stakeholders. Uh, I think the version before you today, reflects a thoughtful citywide approach that expands protections to workers beyond

the city workforce while addressing the concerns that were raised with respect to collective bargaining. It sets a baseline right to leave, it protects workers from retaliation, and it ensures that this benefit can't simply be waived away without something comparable in place. At the end of the day, it's not a partisan issue, it's not an ideological issue, it's a human issue. It's about whether we as a city are going to stand behind people who are willing to do something selfless and sometimes something life-saving. And it's about making sure that doing the right thing doesn't come with a financial penalty. I urge my colleagues and the public to support Intro 831. I thank the Committee sincerely for, uh, its consideration of this bill today. Thank you, Chair.

Thank you, Council Member Morano. Uh, we will now move to the Q&A portion of this this hearing. Um, right before we do that, I just— I wanna thank the Health Committee staff, um, Josh Newman and, um, Elizabeth Arzt and Chris Pepe, who's not here today, the Committee Counsel, and my staff counsel, uh, my Chief of Staff, Jonathan

Boucher, uh, Kevin McAleer, my legislative and budget director, and my comms director, Sammy New. So, um, I wanna start off with, uh, DOHMH. Um, how has the background check process at DOHMH changed since we last had a hearing on this topic in 2023? And can you walk me through the process step by step?

Yes, thank you, Chair. Uh, when we met in 2023, I think— I believe we had only recently launched our online portal, and it's really been a dramatic change since then. And so many of the, uh, the stories that, that you have all told in your opening comments, I think we have move beyond a lot of those issues. Um, so since that time, we now have a staff of, uh, 60, uh, who work solely on background clearances in addition to, um, uh, other staff who have, uh, other roles but who spend some of their time on background clearances. And most importantly, we have an online portal, um, so that providers can enter their background clearances into this portal rather than sending us applications by email. During that period when we were first given this federal mandate in 2019, we were taking in applications by email and literally our, our computer

systems were, were crashing under the weight of those. We launched that system in May 2023, um, and have— things have dramatically improved. So the process is that a person who, uh, will be working with children in child care do two things. They enter their information into our portal, which, like the, uh, provider portal that, ah, er, demonstrated, was designed with input from providers and user testing with providers at the time that we launched a couple of years ago. And you also go to, um, get your fingerprints taken. Another change that was made a couple of years ago is rather than having to go to DOI to get fingerprints, the city entered into a partnership with a private fingerprint provider which has offices all over the region. They have long hours, they are open on the weekends, so that was a big convenience for people to be able to get those fingerprints taken. Um, once those fingerprints have been cleared, um, that person is then able to begin working at the program under the supervision of a fully cleared person. So they don't have to wait until the entire

process has been completed. They can get started working. Meantime, we go through all of the other clearances, uh, the men— you, you cited those, um, in your opening, um, comments. Like the portal that Aaron demonstrated, providers— the applicant has a, ah, an identification number they can type in to check the status of that— of the process. Once those clearances come through, we send a letter to them and to the provider and they can begin working without that, uh, without that supervision.
How much of a backlog exists now?

So, um, our median processing time right now is, uh, about 30 days. There are, uh, there's some seasonality to the application, so there's a kind of, um, peaks to that. So we have had a, a median processing time as low as 20 days, and we're sort of on the downward, uh, slope right now. So we think that processing time will, will, um, get back to that 20-day mark. Um, there are applications that are above 45 days. Our system doesn't allow us to easily tease out what applications are pending with us solely because of our work, as opposed to we

are waiting on an outside state to give us information back. So at any given time, we've got about 500 applications, um, that are beyond the 45-day mark. But those are for a variety of reasons. Some are with us, uh, we are, you know, we're still continuing to make improvements in our turnaround times, as I said. But many of them are because we are waiting for results from out of state, a person who has worked out of state in the prior 5 years. Uh, we need to check those other state, ah, clearance information. Sometimes it takes us longer to get information back from the state central registry than other times, so that can, uh, cause a longer time period for processing. There are times when providers, uh, the applicant has made typos in the application, and so that is something we need to have them correct. We've just recently, about, maybe just a couple of weeks ago, did an upgrade to the system system to have people reenter certain information, which is a common thing that you see in applications. So that will cut down on typos. Um, so those are some of the

reasons but at any given time, that's about how many we have that are beyond the 45-day mark.
And, um, do you have plans— and, ah, er, ah, do you have plans in terms of lowering those 500? I mean, 500 is a lot.

We are continuing to make upgrades to the, uh, to the, ah, portal. So in all of the new releases, there are, there are upgrades that we make that will improve our efficiency. As I said, some of those are outside of our control, and some of those things we are not able to, to change. But we are always looking to see where are there, where are there places where we can, um, speed up some of those processing times. I'll say that when there is a situation where, um, a program is dependent on that clearance in order to operate, say they have an education director that is a, that is a key staff person that you need to be able to operate, if we have an, if they are waiting for that clearance, we will handhold that application and do everything we can to get that through the system faster. So we do maintain constant contact with, uh, with providers, and we try to move those

through as fast as possible. Some of it is outside of our control.
And that portal is separate from the portal that we just saw? So they're two separate portals?
It is, it is. And you saw where AAron pointed out, uh, one of the screenshots where there is integration, but they are separate.

Okay and the integration— I mean, I know it's new, so we'll keep an eye in terms of it working and maybe enhancing the integration and all of that. Okay. Um, hmm, does DOHMH process background checks on behalf of OCFS for state-regulated providers?
So our contract with OCFS, the Office of Children and Family Services, does include, ah, us processing parts of the background clearance for the state-regulated providers.
Okay. How many background check applications across all child care program types are currently pending at DOHMH?

So I can share the city-side information. We're happy to talk to OCFS to, um, see if they will share the data for the state-regulated

programs. Um, at any given time, we get about 3,000 applications a month. Uh, some months are, are busier, so in September, for example, we, we took in 4,200 applications. Um, and right now our median processing time is, is about 30 days. Sometimes it's 20 days. So it, this is a, it is a dynamic, um, uh, er, ah, number, but you can get a sense of what we are, what our, what our docket is at any given time.
Do you have, is there someone that can be spoken to by a provider if they have a problem or there's a glitch or like an ombudsman type person?

Yes. So there's— there are two ways that providers can be in touch with us. Um, the providers have contacts at our borough offices, and they're in pretty regular contact, uh, with the borough offices. But we also have, uh, an, an email inbox that is monitored by several people and is actively, uh, where we actively respond to inquiries.
And providers have that information?

Providers have that. And we have a— we, we've— something we started, um, maybe a year or two ago is we, we not only send out regular

emails to providers with new information, but we've also been doing a monthly roundup of all of the information that's gone out that month. And we've gotten really good feedback about that. So that's another place where they're, they're constantly hearing from us and getting that contact information. And those phone numbers, of course, always live on our website. So if they don't have that, they know to go there.

Is that something that can be added to your portal? Okay. That would be great. Okay. Thank you. Um, how many— oh, I'm sorry. What are the primary drivers of delays in background check processing, staffing, fingerprinting, bottlenecks, interagency coordination? I mean, you sort of mentioned it, but, um—

Yeah, yeah. I mean, for the most part, you know, for, for a sort of healthy application, you could say, um, those clearances are, are very straightforward and they're processed quickly. Every application, um, is, is, uh, er, handled on its own. And, you know, one of the things I didn't mention is that sometimes we do get a report back from one of these, uh, agency checks where there

is something concerning that we need to look into. And so that's another reason that an application may take longer if we have to do an additional assessment to see if that person can work in child care.
So what are the, you know, the things that I mentioned, like, what's maybe the number one kind of driver of a backlog, or they— or it just varies?

I think it really varies. I don't know that there's one or another, and I, and I don't know, I would hesitate to call it a backlog. I mean, a person who has worked out of state in the prior 5 years, and we are doing our due diligence and complying with the law to check that out-of-state history. And we are waiting for that state to report back. I, I would not call that a backlog. Um, so, um, so I would say, and I, and I think all of you have said in your opening remarks, the work that we are doing here is so very important for the providers, for the families, and it's not something where, while we, we feel a tremendous burden to get these done as quickly as possible, we know how critically important it is for the person who will begin work and for the provider who needs that child

care professional in the classroom, but also for the family to make sure that we are not cutting corners.

Okay. Um, in March, Mayor Mamdani announced the expansion of 2K, including the first 2,000 seats coming online this fall and the addition of 1,000 3K seats, is the agency prepared and equipped to process the background checks for the additional providers needed to meet this expanded capacity citywide, and what specific steps have been taken to ensure readiness? Is it on?

Oh, okay. There we go. I'm happy to start with this. So for the expansion of 3K capacity, and the launch of 2K this fall, um, given the relatively quick turnaround time between now and September, the city is planning to work, um, with existing child care providers. So any of the providers who are offering 3K or 2K services this fall already have a license or permit, um, and very likely already have staff in place in those classrooms. We anticipate there will be some new hiring to support 2K and 3K, as there always is in the lead up to the first day of school. But we do not expect a huge rush. We are continuing to monitor what the, uh, staffing patterns will look like with

our partners at New York City Public Schools and with the health department to make sure that we are prepared. And then certainly as we prepare for the fall of 2027, when we will be bringing many more 2K seats online, we'll be planning ahead with the Department of Health and New York City Public Schools to ensure that there is sufficient staff capacity for onboarding those providers.
Okay, thank you. Um, how many background checks does DOHMH process every year for early childhood educators?
Um, so, uh, I can provide the city-side numbers, and that, and that's the numbers I, I gave you before, that 3,000 on a typical month. Some months are bigger. September was 4,200.

Oh, you mentioned that earlier. Okay. Um, to what extent are background check delays contributing to delays in opening new child care slots or programs? So I'm not aware that they are contributing to delays. Any particular program that is having, um, uh, er, experiencing a delay that they think is related to the background clearance should certainly be in touch with our office.

As I noted, the education director, who is a key person to be able to open— is a— is somebody that— that's an application that we handle in our borough office and really handhold because we know that that is the key to being able to open. But we, we would— well, you know, if you, if you are hearing from a, from a provider in your, in your, um, community, please do reach out to us.

Okay. If DOHMH receives a question about an issue that's handled by OCFS, how do you refer that person to OCFS? Is there a clear line of communication for the public to both of you regarding the background check processing?

So for the most part, uh, we can take the those questions. Most of the kinds of questions that come in from providers who are doing a background check, uh, doing that process on the— what we would call the state side, we can answer those questions. If it's something that we cannot answer, we will contact OCFS and make sure that that answer gets back to the provider. Has DOHMH quantified how many providers are unable to begin operations due to pending background

checks, and does DOHMH prioritize the background check of directors so that the business can open?
As we just discussed, yes, we do.

Okay. According to the background check requirements under federal law, a person who has passed the first two fingerprinting checks can work with children if they are never left alone with them. How many people are in this provisional status right now? Hmm.

So really, um, anyone who submits the clearance application and completes those fingerprints and they come back without any concerns, they can begin work so long as they are, um, under the supervision of a fully cleared person. So I don't have that— I don't have that number, but that's something that we were able to provide so that people can at least get started working.

Okay. If you could get it— if you could just get us the number at some point, that would be great. Um, once a person has completed a background check for one employer but chooses to change jobs still within the child care

field,— does that person need to undergo a background check again with the new employer?

So a person who has been fully CBC cleared, so comprehensive background check cleared, mhm, who— and that clearance has been within the past 5 years, and there hasn't been a break in service in 180 days, if they want to change employers-
Right.
Then what they need to do is let us know in the portal that they are changing locations.
Mhm.

And then they are good to go. Um, we will, uh, move their fingerprints over to this new— this is sort of in the, on the, on the back end. They, this is invisible to the, ah, child care professional. We will attach the, the fingerprint to their new employer. And there are a couple of the clearances that we will repeat, but that is invisible, um, to the provider, um, and to the, uh, to the applicant themselves. They can begin working as soon as they just let us know.
Okay. How does DOHMH work with DOE to see whether an educator has already passed the two clearances necessary for working with DOE and with DOHMH?

So this is another thing that we have done a, a lot of work on, probably since the last time we— mhm— met, which is that we, um, we do now have access to the DOE system. So we are able to— someone who has those fingerprints completed for DOE, we are able to essentially use those in our system.

Now, I know, um, well, we had DOE here for another hearing, and they, they meant— they mentioned that, and they seemed to— you guys seem to be able to work really well together, from what I could gather. Um, how does DOHMH track and report processing timelines internally, and are there established benchmarks or service-level targets?

We do have, um, internal metrics to, um, measure the— our turnaround times. Um, and, you know, certainly we are— our primary goal is never to exceed that federal mandate for the work that is in our control. So that 45-day mandate for the work

that we are doing ourselves. And otherwise, our goal is to get that number down, our, our processing time down as quickly as we can.
Are there disparities in approval timelines between home-based providers, which are regulated through OCFS, and center-based providers, which are regulated through DOHMH?
So we're happy to pass on the question to OCFS to get the— the processing time information from them.

And then I wanna know, like, what are the diff— what's driving the differences, if there are differences. Okay. At the Council's last hearing on this issue in 2023, DOHMH testified that the agency was onboarding 40 new staff members to process background check applications. How many staff— you said there's about 60, right, to address background check? Okay. And do you have any vacancies in the unit right now?

We, we have just normal attrition, um, so, I, you know, nothing that is staff shortages. And as you, as you heard Emmy said, um, you know, we are, we're working very closely together

to make sure that as the city, um, expands providers, that we will likewise expand.
So given the recent announcement of, again, of the 2K and 3K expansion, does DOHMH need additional funding for additional staff to process the background check?

So we, we don't need funding now, um, and, um, and as you know from our, from our budget hearing, we did get, um, resources just even anticipating some of the initial expansion, um, that you just heard about. Um, but we are working very closely together to make sure that as the city's provider, ah, capacity expands, that our capacity will expand alongside that.

Okay, great and we have our executive budget hearing coming up, so anticipate some questions. Um, what are the costs associated with conducting a background check excluding fingerprinting, and who's responsible for covering these costs?
Do you mean the agent's— the Health Department's costs to administer the program? Is that—

Um, what are the costs associated with cutting— er, with conducting a background check, um, my, uh, so what I'm asking is who's responsible? The agency, the provider, the individual undergoing the background check? Like, are there questions-
You mean to pay for the fingerprinting?
To do the— well, excluding the fingerprinting.
Excluding the fingerprinting.
Is there anything, or there's not?
I don't think there's a cost to submit the background clearance.

Okay. Is DOHMH open to increasing transparency for providers around the status of their background check for themselves or their employees? Well, you, you already— you already— by creating a portal such as, um, the Mayor's Office of Child Care has done for the new permits.

So we do have a portal that we launched in May, uh, I think it was May 22nd. It was

a big day, so I remember the date, 2023. And, um, applicants can— they are given a— a number, um, of an application number, and so they are able to type that in and get, uh, to check the status of the application, and we also do email them.
When a potential early childhood educator fails a background check, how is this communicated to them, and how is it communicated to the potential employer?

So a letter does go out. Um, there are obviously confidentiality issues here, so different information goes to, um, the applicant and the provider in some cases, but there is a letter that goes, um, um, and including, you know, if they're— including information about, ah, next steps for the applicant if they want to, for example, appeal that decision or give us more information.
Okay. For those potential early childhood educators who do not speak English as a first language, do you offer translation services for those undergoing the background check process?

So our background check portal, uh, is able to be translated. So, um, there is, uh, there's language accessibility there. And for people

who have questions who wanna contact either their borough office or, um, to speak to the central office, we can always use LanguageLine and our staff are trained to do that.
Do you know how many languages is served or—
By LanguageLine?
Mhm.
It's many. 200.

Okay. No, that's great. Um, now I'm, I'm gonna, um, I appreciate this and, um, I'm gonna ask Chair Gutiérrez, uh, for questions on her end. Thank, thank you very much. Appreciate it. CHAIRPERSON GUTIÉRREZ: Thank you, Chair Schulman. And I, I do have a couple, a number of questions for, for Emmy again. Um, but I just, I did have some follow-up questions for you, Deputy Commissioner. Thank you so much for answering everything. Let me just make sure I have my notes. Um, what is— can you just, uh, uh, to start, um, clarify the 30-day timeline? Is that, um, from the, the, the fingerprint process with DOI, or is that like sep— that is only once kind of you get notified?

What is that? What is the— when does the clock start that you're timing for the 30 days?

So that median time will be from when the time that somebody submits the application to us. Whether they have already gone and gotten their fingerprints, I don't, I, I don't know. You could, you could do it either way. You can come to us, you could start entering after you've already gotten the fingerprints. CHAIRPERSON GUTIÉRREZ: Sure. Okay. Okay. That's helpful. I think that's it. Okay. Um, so you, you referenced kind of some of the, the areas that you have, that the agency has improved on. Um, what is, I guess, what kind of a delay is a typo? Put— like, what is the level of a strain that a typo— and, you know, tell me, because on my end I'm like, a typo takes seconds. But what is— I don't know, is a typo like, I put the wrong initial here, I put a period where it wasn't supposed to go? Like, because that— it seems like a significant— it seems like a significant enough error where it's creating a delay. But what is the turnaround on that?

So it's, it's an example of the kind of thing where if we get a, uh, what we would

call a healthy the application, we can handle that much more quickly. If you've reversed numbers in your Social Security number, that's gonna delay, you know, all these checks are dependent on that Social Security number. We don't know that there's been a typo in your Social Security number. So, um, that's just the sort of thing, and 45 days is not a lot of time, so any of these couple of day issues, mhm, uh, can, can, you know, extend the timeline. CHAIRPERSON GUTIÉRREZ: And then you— thank you— and then you did mention- Well, I'm just curious back on the typo. Is, is, um, so it's not, it's not necessarily like spelling errors. It's like technical errors like this. Like, is that—
Yeah, so a date of birth. CHAIRPERSON GUTIÉRREZ: Okay, yeah.

If you, if you reverse your date of birth, you know, the, the date, and so we don't have the correct date of birth, then that's gonna, that's something we, we may not discover. So this, we, as I said, we just a couple of weeks ago did a new release where we have you enter that twice. That's a way to reduce those kinds of errors. I don't know yet how helpful that is because we just

released it, but that's the sort of thing as we gain more and more experience, we can see what are the kinds of things that are tripping people up that we can fix with technology and just eliminate those. CHAIRPERSON GUTIÉRREZ: Okay. And— okay. I think that that was— I, I, I think I have some more, but I think that that's it just based on your responses. Thank you so much. Um, I had some questions for the Mayor's office and certainly want to hear from you, Aaron. Thank you for, for walking us through this. I think it looks really good. Also, I don't know if you've gotten any credit for just the layout of it. I think sometimes, you know, it's hard to put together these, um, new sites and expect everyone to just jump in and fully understand it. But I think the layout is really, really easy, really forward. And I really appreciate that you were able to work with providers to put this together. Um, just based on this though, can you clarify, are these for new applicants or new applicants and existing applicants?
Currently it is for new— it's for prelims, what we call new applicants for group daycare. CHAIRPERSON GUTIÉRREZ: Okay.

Um, we do have plans to expand it to renewals. That is, in fact, we're talking with DOH right now to get those business rules, and we plan to, you know, that I think will be our next big release because I know there's a huge demand for renewals and amendments as well. Currently right now it is just prelims, new applicants. CHAIRPERSON GUTIÉRREZ: Okay. And is there anything that folks should know about— this is really wonky— but about uploading docs? Because I think oftentimes, I'll use the example of 311, you can't necessarily upload a doc or a picture if the resolution is too low, or, you know, it just— if I'm, you know, someone who's interested in opening up, opening up a group daycare and I don't know this, how easy is it for them to upload documents, to, you know, or pictures that they need to— like, what is that communication with them while they're already here so that we don't lose them?

Right, right. So in— you see in the screenshot there, we actually give some instructions like, look, we accept these kind of files. PDF is one, JPEG is another. A lot of people just take pictures of their documents and as long as it's— as long as you can read it, that, that can count. So we try to give them that and we try to give them a document size limit, it's fairly large. You'd have to do that. So we give them that upfront. Some people are going to have issues, you know, with that and what have you. There is, you know, there is a— there's sort of like a contact support thing if you're having trouble uploading a document. Um, so we can, you know, that will go to a help desk who can try to support them. But usually we try to tell them up front. We're finding, at least when we spoke to providers, it's going to happen Council Member, obviously. But like, it's, it's the same sort of requirements that they're kind of used to at this point with when they're uploading documents at their bank. Or any of the other things. It's often the

same requirements. But you're right, it can be, it can be, uh, a point of failure. CHAIRPERSON GUTIÉRREZ: And is the idea that once these new providers are utilizing this site that they will continue to use this site every couple of years?

Yeah, we'd like— we're really trying to design it so it's not just a one and go. Like, the— but we hope those providers can stay in business and grow and prosper. So they're going to renew. We're going to have renewals ready by then. We have some information such as that background check. CHAIRPERSON GUTIÉRREZ: So everyone at some— every home-based provider at some point will have to be transitioned to using this site?
That's correct. CHAIRPERSON GUTIÉRREZ: Okay, okay.
I'm sorry? Center-based. Center-based, yeah. CHAIRPERSON GUTIÉRREZ: What about— what did I say? Home-based. Center-based. My bad. No, no, no, no. We got to clarify, thank you.

I just heard center. Thank you. Home-based is state, and I— we would love to automate the state system. CHAIRPERSON GUTIÉRREZ: No, no, no, no. I want to be clear. I don't want to confuse anyone. Thank you, Emmy. Okay. Great. Um, okay and besides this— besides, ah, this new site, is My City only going to be used for for this to the, to the best of our knowledge?
You wanna take that? CHAIRPERSON GUTIÉRREZ: In its, its new iteration?

So MyCity has both a parent-facing, um, portal and a provider-facing portal. Um, the parent-facing portal for MyCity is how families are able to apply and recertify for child care vouchers. Um, and the provider-facing side is where the provider portal lives. So both of those functions continue to be maintained. CHAIRPERSON GUTIÉRREZ: Okay. Just for— and that's— that's fine, but just for the purpose of child care at this point. Yes. Okay. Great. Um, thank you.

And are— for, for you all, and I know that this is obviously, like, part of the process, are there other ways, I mean, that your team is working with DOHMH to identify efficiencies or greater transparency in the background check process?

Um, so we collaborate very closely with DOHMH and, um, with Deputy Commissioner's team, we meet on a weekly or biweekly basis to discuss and troubleshoot things that we are hearing from providers, things that, um, we are observing in our regular work.
